title: Sandbox Demo for IT Management Software: Let Admins Click Through Without a Test Tenant
summary: A sandbox demo for IT management software lets admins click through your console without a test tenant or enrolled devices. Storylane's SE playbook.
body_markdown:
If you sell IT management or endpoint-management software and want a sandbox demo admins can actually use, you already know the moment I am talking about. An IT admin says "can I just click around in it?" and the honest answer is "yes, after we spin up a tenant, you install an agent, enroll a couple of devices, wait for inventory to populate, and give it a few days." By then the admin has moved on to a vendor whose product they could see in five minutes.


Here is the position I will defend: for IT and endpoint-management vendors, the first hands-on experience should not require a test tenant or enrolled devices at all. It should be a sandbox demo, a clickable clone of your console that is already full of realistic devices, deployments and patch states. The tenant and the agent install still matter, but they belong in the proof of concept, not at the front door.


I'm Madhav, CMO at Storylane. This piece is written for sales engineers and presales leads at IT management vendors. It is deliberately narrower than our general[SE guide to demo environment types](https://www.storylane.io/blog/the-ses-guide-to-demo-environment-types) : that guide covers which environment fits which situation across any SaaS product. This one is about one specific problem, which is that your product only looks alive once devices are reporting into it.


## Why endpoint-management software is uniquely hard to demo


Most SaaS products can be demoed from a fresh account with a bit of seeded data. Endpoint and IT management products cannot, for a structural reason: the value lives in the fleet. An empty console with zero devices, zero deployment history and zero compliance findings tells the admin nothing about whether your product will make Tuesday patch day less painful.


To get a real tenant to look like a real environment, someone has to do work that has nothing to do with selling:


- **Provision a tenant or trial instance** , often with license keys, region selection and admin accounts.
- **Install an agent or enrollment profile** on physical machines or virtual machines, which many corporate security teams will not allow on a whim.
- **Wait for inventory and reporting** to populate, so dashboards show something other than empty states.
- **Create history** : past deployments, failed installs, out-of-date software, policy drift. Without history, reporting screens are blank.
- **Clean up afterwards** , because trial tenants accumulate stale devices and test data that confuse the next prospect.


Every one of those steps is friction for the buyer and capacity drain for the SE. And the friction lands at the worst point in the cycle: before the buyer has decided you are worth that effort.


## What a sandbox demo actually is (and is not)


A sandbox demo, in the way Storylane uses the term on its[sandbox demo page](https://www.storylane.io/sandbox-demo) , is a working clone of your product that buyers can click through freely rather than following a fixed path. It captures live HTML rather than screenshots, so hovers, dropdowns and modals behave as they do in the real product. You record it once by clicking through your console, and buttons link to the screens they open.


For an IT management product, that means the admin can open the device list, filter by operating system, click into a machine, look at installed software, open a deployment, and see a patch compliance report, all without a single real device enrolled anywhere.


What it is not:


- It is **not a backend** . Nothing actually deploys. A script does not run on a real machine. A policy does not reach a real laptop.
- It is **not an integration test** . It cannot prove your product works with the buyer's directory, identity provider or network topology.
- It is **not a substitute for a proof of concept** when the buyer needs to validate behaviour in their own environment.


That distinction is the whole game. The sandbox answers "what is it like to use this console?" The tenant answers "does it work on our machines?" Those are different questions asked at different stages, and conflating them is how SE teams end up provisioning tenants for buyers who were only ever going to look around.


## The old way vs. the sandbox-first way


Step in the cycle Tenant-first motion Sandbox-first motion


Admin asks to "click around" SE provisions a trial tenant, sends agent install instructions SE sends a sandbox link the same day


What the admin sees first Empty dashboards until devices check in A populated console with realistic devices, deployments and reports


Who has to approve something Buyer's security team, before an agent goes on any machine Nobody, because nothing installs


Live call reliability Depends on tenant state, network, and what changed since last week Behaves the same on every call


When the tenant is used From the first hands-on touch Only in the POC, for buyers who have already shortlisted you


SE time per early-stage evaluator High (setup, troubleshooting, cleanup) Low (send, personalize, follow up on engagement)


This is a directional comparison, not a benchmark. The point is where the effort sits: the tenant-first motion front-loads SE work onto buyers who have not yet qualified themselves.


## Who inside the buyer actually clicks, and what they need to see


IT management purchases are rarely made by one person. The sandbox has to work for several roles, and each one is looking for a different screen. Design the sandbox around these jobs rather than around your navigation menu.


Role at the buyer What they want to verify Screens to make sure are captured


Hands-on sysadmin or desktop engineer Daily workflows feel fast and predictable Device list, device detail, software deployment, scheduling, results and retries


IT manager Visibility across the fleet and the team Dashboards, compliance and patch status reports, filters and saved views


Security or compliance stakeholder Control and auditability Role-based access screens, audit or activity views, policy settings


Budget owner That the team will actually adopt it A short guided path that shows the core outcome in a few clicks


Notice that the budget owner needs a different experience from the sysadmin. That is why many teams pair a free-roam sandbox with a short guided demo, rather than handing everyone the same open console.


## Keep the guided path short, even for a technical product


There is a temptation, when your buyer is technical, to show everything. Storylane's own first-party analysis argues against that. In[our analysis of demo lengths across 9 industries](https://www.storylane.io/blog/learnings-from-analyzing-demo-lengths-across-9-industries) (a small sample: 34 website demos and 5,409 demo sessions), the bottom three industries by completion (Cloud, Cyber Security and Data) averaged a 10.7% completion rate with an average of 43 steps. The top three (Product, Marketing and Sales tech) averaged 41% completion at an average of 11 steps.


That analysis covered website demos, not sandboxes used on live calls, and the sample is small, so treat it as a direction rather than a law. But the direction matches what you would expect: technical vendors build long tours because there is a lot to show, and fewer people finish them. The practical takeaway for an IT management SE is to split the job in two. Give the evaluator a short guided path to the core outcome, then let them roam the sandbox for depth.


## A real IT software example: what PDQ measured


The clearest public example I can point to in this category is PDQ, which describes itself on its customer story as building endpoint management software for IT professionals.[PDQ's customer story](https://www.storylane.io/customer-stories/how-pdq-proved-a-92-conversion-lift-from-their-storylane-demo) is worth reading in full, and I want to be precise about what it does and does not say.


According to that story:


- PDQ's audience is described as technical and skeptical, wanting to see products for themselves before making decisions. Buyers can sign up for a trial, schedule a demo with an AE, or purchase directly from the website.
- The interactive demo was positioned as a pre-trial education asset, meant to help a technical buyer understand the value proposition before raising their hand.
- The core measurement was a before-and-after cohort comparison of site-wide conversion: a 3.19% average conversion rate without Storylane versus 6.14% with it, a 92% lift, and the story reports that this held across eight months of data.
- The story reports that 1 in 5 visitors engages with the demo each month.
- PDQ also ran an A/B test on a paid landing page, putting the Storylane demo against a video in the same placement, and the demo version won.


Two honest caveats. First, this was a product tour on PDQ's website, owned by product marketing, not an SE-run sandbox on live calls. Second, a before-and-after comparison is not a controlled experiment, and the story itself frames it as a cohort analysis. I include it because it is a real IT management vendor showing that a technical, skeptical admin audience will engage with a clickable demo before ever touching a trial. That is exactly the behaviour a sandbox-first SE motion relies on.


## Illustrative worked example: sizing the SE time you get back


*The numbers below are hypothetical and exist only to show the arithmetic. Replace them with your own.*


Imagine an SE team at an endpoint-management vendor that provisions a trial tenant for every evaluator who asks for hands-on access. Assume:


- 30 hands-on requests per month across the team (illustrative).
- About 3 hours of SE time per request for tenant setup, agent install support, a troubleshooting call and cleanup (illustrative).
- Only a third of those evaluators go on to a real POC (illustrative).


That is 90 SE hours a month, of which roughly 60 hours go to evaluators who never reach a POC. If a sandbox link handles the "can I click around?" request and the tenant is reserved for the third who shortlist you, the same team spends tenant time on 10 evaluators instead of 30. Even after adding time to personalize and follow up on sandboxes, the freed capacity is meaningful, and it moves to deals that are actually progressing.


Your real numbers will differ. The structure of the calculation will not: count the tenants you provision for people who never reach a POC, and that is your addressable waste.


## How to build the sandbox for an IT management console


1. **Start from a clean, well-populated internal environment.** Use your best internal demo tenant, the one with a realistic mix of operating systems, failed and successful deployments, and a patch report that shows something to fix.
2. **Capture the daily workflows first.** Device list, device detail, deploy a package, view results, run a report. These are the screens the sysadmin will judge you on.
3. **Replace anything sensitive.** Storylane's sandbox editor lets you blur PII and edit text and elements, and its sandbox page describes AI-generated realistic demo data so no real customer records are needed. Hostnames, usernames and IP ranges from a real internal environment should not ship to prospects.
4. **Personalize per account.** Text and image tokens can swap company names, logos and other values, so the device names and org name can reflect the prospect. A console that looks like their fleet lands harder than a generic one.
5. **Add a short guided path on top.** Five to ten steps to the core outcome for the budget owner and IT manager, with the free-roam sandbox behind it for the hands-on engineer.
6. **Gate it appropriately.** IT buyers are security-minded, and so are you. Storylane lists password, expiry and email-domain restrictions for sandbox demos. Our guide to[securing your product demo for enterprise sales](https://www.storylane.io/blog/secure-your-product-demo-for-enterprise-sales) covers this in more depth.
7. **Recapture when the console changes.** When you ship a UI update, recapture only the screens that changed rather than rebuilding the whole demo.


## Where a sandbox stops and the tenant starts


I am not arguing that you should never provision a tenant. For endpoint management, the POC is where the buyer validates the things a front-end clone cannot: agent behaviour on their own images, deployment success rates on their network, integration with their directory and identity stack, and performance at their scale. Those are real technical risks and a sandbox does not retire them.


We wrote a separate, candid piece on[when sandbox demos don't work](https://www.storylane.io/blog/when-sandbox-demos-dont-work) , and it applies here. If the buyer's core question is "will your agent coexist with our existing security tooling?" no amount of clicking through a cloned console answers it.


A simple rule of thumb for IT management SEs:


The buyer's question Right tool


What does the console look like day to day? Sandbox demo


How would my team deploy and patch with this? Sandbox demo, ideally personalized to their fleet


Can my manager see the reporting before we commit time? Short guided demo plus sandbox link


Does the agent work on our machines and network? Tenant and POC


Does it integrate with our identity and directory setup? Tenant and POC


Will it perform at our device count? Tenant and POC, with your engineering team involved


For security-adjacent buyers, the sequencing question is similar, and our companion piece on[security tool evaluation before the POC](https://www.storylane.io/blog/security-tool-evaluation-before-poc) walks through it.


## Where Storylane fits (full disclosure)


Storylane is a demo platform, so I have an obvious interest here. What follows is limited to what our[sandbox demo page](https://www.storylane.io/sandbox-demo) states today.


- **Capture:** record an HTML demo of your product using the Chrome extension or desktop app; buttons auto-link to screens as you click, and you can link screens manually where needed.
- **Editing:** a no-code editor to change text and elements, blur sensitive PII and modify HTML elements, plus an AI editor that takes prompts for changes to charts, tables, text and data.
- **Demo data:** AI-generated realistic demo data so real records and PII do not leave your systems.
- **Personalization:** text and image tokens for names, logos, currencies and dates, and personalized sandbox links to track engagement.
- **Live calls:** presenter notes visible only to you, keyed to each screen.
- **Access control and enterprise:** password, expiry and email-domain restrictions; custom domain, SSO, whitelabel and SOC 2 compliance are listed on the same page.
- **Plan:** sandbox demos are built on HTML recordings and require the Growth plan or above. Screenshot-based interactive demos are available on all plans, including free.


What Storylane does not do is run your backend. If your POC requires a functioning agent talking to a live server, that is a tenant, and you should plan for it.


## How to measure whether sandbox-first is working


Pick a small set of metrics you can defend, which is the same discipline PDQ's story describes for its reporting. For an SE team, I would track:


- **Tenants provisioned per month, and the share that reach a POC.** Sandbox-first should reduce the first number and raise the second.
- **Time from hands-on request to first hands-on experience.** Same-day should become normal.
- **Sandbox engagement by account** : who opened it, which screens they reached, and whether more than one person from the buying group viewed it.
- **Stage conversion from evaluation to POC** , compared against a period before the change, with the caveat that a before-and-after comparison is not a controlled test.
- **SE hours on tenant setup and cleanup.** This is the cost you are trying to remove.


## Common mistakes


- **Capturing an empty tenant.** If your recording environment has three devices and no history, your sandbox inherits the empty-state problem. Populate first, then capture.
- **Shipping real hostnames and usernames.** Internal environments leak details. Blur or replace before anything goes to a prospect.
- **Handing the budget owner the full console.** Give them a short guided path. Save free-roam for the engineer.
- **Using the sandbox to dodge the POC.** If the buyer's question is about agent behaviour or integration, say so and schedule the POC.
- **Letting the sandbox drift from the release.** If the buyer later sees a different UI in the tenant, you lose credibility. Recapture changed screens when you ship.


## The bottom line


For IT and endpoint-management vendors, the hardest part of the demo is not the story, it is the fleet. A tenant with enrolled devices is the only way to prove the product works on the buyer's machines, but it is an expensive and slow way to answer the much more common question of what the console is like to use. Answer that question with a sandbox the same day, keep the guided path short, and reserve tenants for the buyers who have earned a POC.

## FAQ


### Can IT admins try endpoint-management software without a test tenant?


Yes, for the question of how the console works. A sandbox demo is a clickable clone of the product, captured as HTML, so admins can browse devices, deployments and reports without any device being enrolled. Validating agent behaviour on their own machines still requires a tenant and a proof of concept.


### Does a sandbox demo actually deploy software or patches?


No. A sandbox demo replicates the front end of your product. Clicking deploy shows the screens that follow, but nothing runs on a real machine. That is why it suits early evaluation and live calls, not technical validation.


### How do you make a sandbox look like a real fleet?


Capture from a well-populated internal environment with a realistic mix of devices, deployment history and patch findings, then replace sensitive details. Storylane supports blurring PII, editing elements, AI-generated demo data and tokens for personalizing names and logos per prospect.


### When should an SE still provision a trial tenant?


When the buyer needs to validate agent behaviour on their own images, integration with their directory or identity setup, network conditions or performance at their scale. Those are POC questions, best reserved for shortlisted buyers.


### Which Storylane plan includes sandbox demos?


According to Storylane's sandbox demo page, sandbox demos are built on HTML recordings and require the Growth plan or above. Screenshot-based interactive demos are available on all plans, including free.
